```{r}
#| label: complete-analysis
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
df <- readr::read_csv("data/online_shoppers_intention.csv",show_col_types=FALSE)
df$Duration_Minutes <- df$ProductRelated_Duration/60
df$Log_Duration <- log1p(df$Duration_Minutes)
df_clean <- df |> filter(VisitorType %in% c("New_Visitor","Returning_Visitor")) |>
  mutate(Revenue=as.integer(Revenue),
    VisitorType=factor(VisitorType,levels=c("New_Visitor","Returning_Visitor")),
    across(c(OperatingSystems,Browser,Region,TrafficType,Month),factor),
    Weekend=factor(Weekend,levels=c(FALSE,TRUE)))
model1 <- glm(Revenue~Duration_Minutes+VisitorType+ProductRelated+Weekend,data=df_clean,family=binomial())
model2 <- glm(Revenue~Duration_Minutes*VisitorType+ProductRelated+Weekend,data=df_clean,family=binomial())

library(car)
library(pROC)
library(ResourceSelection)
library(splines)
dir.create("outputs/diagnostics", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 10))
visitor_labels <- c(New_Visitor = "New visitors", Returning_Visitor = "Returning visitors")
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))

# Broader adjustment is motivated by professor feedback, not univariate p-values.
# Frequency-only pooling prevents very small traffic categories with zero purchases.
d_assess <- df_clean
traffic_n <- table(d_assess$TrafficType)
d_assess$TrafficGroup <- factor(ifelse(traffic_n[as.character(d_assess$TrafficType)] < 100,
                                      "Other", as.character(d_assess$TrafficType)))
d_assess$Month <- relevel(d_assess$Month, ref = "May")
stopifnot(nrow(d_assess) == 12245, all(d_assess$Revenue %in% 0:1), !anyNA(d_assess))
f3 <- Revenue ~ Duration_Minutes * VisitorType + ProductRelated + Weekend +
  Administrative + Informational + ExitRates + Month + TrafficGroup
f4 <- Revenue ~ Log_Duration * VisitorType + ProductRelated + Weekend +
  Administrative + Informational + ExitRates + Month + TrafficGroup
f5 <- Revenue ~ splines::ns(Log_Duration, df = 3) * VisitorType + ProductRelated +
  Weekend + Administrative + Informational + ExitRates + Month + TrafficGroup
model3 <- glm(f3, data = d_assess, family = binomial())
model4 <- glm(f4, data = d_assess, family = binomial())
model5 <- glm(f5, data = d_assess, family = binomial())
model3_nointer <- glm(update(f3, . ~ . - Duration_Minutes:VisitorType), data = d_assess, family = binomial())
model4_nointer <- glm(update(f4, . ~ . - Log_Duration:VisitorType), data = d_assess, family = binomial())
model5_nointer <- glm(Revenue ~ splines::ns(Log_Duration, df = 3) + VisitorType +
  ProductRelated + Weekend + Administrative + Informational + ExitRates + Month + TrafficGroup,
  data = d_assess, family = binomial())
model5_noexit <- glm(update(f5, . ~ . - ExitRates), data = d_assess, family = binomial())
model5_admin <- glm(update(f5, . ~ . - Administrative +
  splines::ns(Administrative, knots = c(1,5))), data = d_assess, family = binomial())
models_assess <- list(M1 = model1, M2 = model2, M3 = model3, M4 = model4, M5 = model5)
null_assess <- glm(Revenue ~ 1, data = d_assess, family = binomial())
fit_metrics <- bind_rows(lapply(names(models_assess), function(nm) {
  m <- models_assess[[nm]]
  hl <- ResourceSelection::hoslem.test(d_assess$Revenue, fitted(m), g = 10)
  tibble(Model = nm, Parameters = length(coef(m)), Deviance = deviance(m), AIC = AIC(m),
    McFadden = 1 - as.numeric(logLik(m)/logLik(null_assess)),
    AUC = as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(d_assess$Revenue, fitted(m), levels=c(0,1), direction="<", quiet=TRUE))),
    HL_statistic = unname(hl$statistic), HL_df = unname(hl$parameter), HL_p = hl$p.value)
}))
lrt_row <- function(label, reduced, full) {
  a <- anova(reduced, full, test="Chisq")
  tibble(Comparison=label, df=a$Df[2], LR=a$Deviance[2], p=a$`Pr(>Chi)`[2])
}
interaction_tests <- bind_rows(lrt_row("M1 vs M2: raw-duration interaction",model1,model2),
  lrt_row("M3: expanded raw-duration interaction",model3_nointer,model3),
  lrt_row("M4: expanded log-duration interaction",model4_nointer,model4),
  lrt_row("M5: joint nonlinear interaction",model5_nointer,model5))
# All LR tests below compare nested models on the same observations. Raw vs log
# specifications are NON-nested; compare their AIC, never an LR test between them.
m2_duration_flex <- glm(Revenue ~ splines::ns(Duration_Minutes,3)*VisitorType +
  ProductRelated + Weekend, data=d_assess, family=binomial())
m2_pages_flex <- glm(Revenue ~ Duration_Minutes*VisitorType +
  splines::ns(ProductRelated,3) + Weekend, data=d_assess, family=binomial())
functional_tests <- bind_rows(lrt_row("M2: nonlinear duration by visitor",model2,m2_duration_flex),
  lrt_row("M2: nonlinear product page count",model2,m2_pages_flex),
  lrt_row("M4 vs M5: remaining duration curvature",model4,model5))
for (v in c("ProductRelated","Administrative","Informational","ExitRates")) {
  knots <- switch(v, ProductRelated="10,40", Administrative="1,5", Informational="1,2", ExitRates="0.01,0.05")
  ff <- update(f5, paste(". ~ . -",v,"+ splines::ns(",v,", knots=c(",knots,"))"))
  mm <- glm(ff,data=d_assess,family=binomial())
  functional_tests <- bind_rows(functional_tests,lrt_row(paste("M5: curvature in",v),model5,mm))
}

# VIF for the main-effects model isolates predictor overlap; the interaction
# model's term VIF also reflects how interaction columns are constructed.
vif_main <- tibble(Predictor=names(car::vif(model1)), VIF=as.numeric(car::vif(model1)))
vif_interaction <- tibble(Predictor=names(car::vif(model2)), VIF=as.numeric(car::vif(model2)))
v5 <- car::vif(model5)
vif_proposed <- tibble(Term=rownames(v5), GVIF=v5[,1], df=v5[,2], adjusted_GVIF=v5[,3])
predictor_cor <- cor(d_assess[,c("Duration_Minutes","Log_Duration","ProductRelated","Administrative","Informational","ExitRates")])

# Convergence / separation screen. This is a numerical screen, not an LP proof.
numerical_checks <- bind_rows(lapply(names(models_assess),function(nm) {
  m <- models_assess[[nm]]
  refit <- glm(formula(m),data=d_assess,family=binomial(),control=glm.control(maxit=100,epsilon=1e-10))
  tibble(Model=nm,Converged=m$converged, Boundary=m$boundary,
    Rank=m$rank, Columns=ncol(model.matrix(m)), Max_SE=max(sqrt(diag(vcov(m)))),
    Extreme_probabilities=sum(fitted(m)<1e-8 | fitted(m)>1-1e-8),
    Max_refit_change=max(abs(coef(refit)-coef(m))))
}))
category_support <- bind_rows(lapply(c("VisitorType","Weekend","Month","TrafficGroup"),function(v) {
  d_assess |> group_by(Level=.data[[v]]) |> summarise(No_purchase=sum(Revenue==0),Purchase=sum(Revenue==1),.groups="drop") |>
    mutate(Variable=v,Level=as.character(Level))
}))

# Component-plus-working-residual plots, as in the course's HW6. The duration
# component includes the interaction contribution for each visitor group.
make_partial <- function(m, data, exposure, pages="ProductRelated") {
  b <- coef(m); inter <- grep(paste0(exposure,":VisitorType|VisitorType.*:",exposure),names(b),value=TRUE)
  slope <- b[exposure] + if(length(inter)) ifelse(data$VisitorType=="Returning_Visitor",b[inter],0) else 0
  bind_rows(tibble(Visitor=data$VisitorType,Variable=ifelse(exposure=="Duration_Minutes","Duration (minutes)","Log(1 + duration in minutes)"),
    X=data[[exposure]], Partial=residuals(m,type="working")+slope*data[[exposure]]),
    tibble(Visitor=data$VisitorType,Variable="Product pages (count)",X=data[[pages]],
      Partial=residuals(m,type="working")+b[pages]*data[[pages]]))
}
partial_initial <- make_partial(model2,d_assess,"Duration_Minutes")
partial_log <- make_partial(model4,d_assess,"Log_Duration")
partial_plot <- function(z,title) {
  z |> group_by(Variable) |> filter(X <= quantile(X,.99)) |> ungroup() |>
    ggplot(aes(X,Partial,color=Visitor)) + geom_point(alpha=.04,size=.5) +
    geom_smooth(method="loess",formula=y~x,se=FALSE,linewidth=.7) +
    geom_smooth(method="lm",formula=y~x,se=FALSE,linetype=2,linewidth=.5) +
    facet_wrap(~Variable,scales="free_x") + coord_cartesian(ylim=c(-8,8)) +
    scale_color_manual(values=c("#156082","#BD582C"),labels=visitor_labels) +
    labs(title=title,x=NULL,y="Component + working residual",color=NULL,
      caption="LOESS (solid) and linear guide (dashed); 99th-percentile x display, y clipped for readability. All sessions used in models.") +
    theme(legend.position="bottom",plot.caption=element_text(size=7))
}
partial_initial_plot <- partial_plot(partial_initial,"Original interaction model: functional-form check")
partial_log_plot <- partial_plot(partial_log,"Expanded log-duration model: remaining curvature")

diagnostic_rows <- bind_rows(lapply(c("M2","M5"),function(nm) {
  m<-models_assess[[nm]]
  tibble(Model=nm,Row=seq_len(nrow(d_assess)),Fitted=fitted(m),
    Deviance_residual=residuals(m,type="deviance"),Pearson_residual=residuals(m,type="pearson"),
    Cooks_distance=cooks.distance(m),Leverage=hatvalues(m))
}))
residual_plot <- ggplot(diagnostic_rows,aes(Fitted,Deviance_residual)) +
  geom_point(alpha=.05,size=.5) + geom_hline(yintercept=0,linetype=2) + facet_wrap(~Model) +
  labs(x="Fitted purchase probability",y="Deviance residual")
cook_plot <- ggplot(diagnostic_rows,aes(Row,Cooks_distance)) + geom_point(alpha=.3,size=.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept=4/nrow(d_assess),color="#BD582C",linetype=2) + facet_wrap(~Model,scales="free_y") +
  labs(x="Analytical row number",y="Cook's distance")
influence_summary <- diagnostic_rows |> group_by(Model) |> summarise(
  Flagged=sum(Cooks_distance>4/nrow(d_assess)),Max_Cook=max(Cooks_distance),
  Most_influential=Row[which.max(Cooks_distance)],Max_leverage=max(Leverage),.groups="drop")

# Interpretable finite contrasts use the full covariance matrix, including spline
# basis covariances. Coefficients of spline bases are NOT per-minute odds ratios.
duration_contrast <- function(m,visitor,from=10,to=20) {
  nd<-d_assess[rep(1,2),,drop=FALSE]
  nd$VisitorType<-factor(rep(visitor,2),levels=levels(d_assess$VisitorType))
  nd$Duration_Minutes<-c(from,to);nd$Log_Duration<-log1p(c(from,to))
  X<-model.matrix(delete.response(terms(m)),model.frame(delete.response(terms(m)),nd,xlev=m$xlevels),contrasts.arg=m$contrasts)
  delta<-X[2,]-X[1,];est<-sum(delta*coef(m));se<-sqrt(drop(delta %*% vcov(m) %*% delta))
  tibble(Visitor=visitor,From=from,To=to,Log_OR=est,SE_log_OR=se,OR=exp(est),
    Lower=exp(est-1.96*se),Upper=exp(est+1.96*se),p=2*pnorm(-abs(est/se)))
}
contrast_table <- bind_rows(lapply(c("M2","M3","M4","M5"),function(nm) {
  bind_rows(lapply(levels(d_assess$VisitorType),function(v) duration_contrast(models_assess[[nm]],v))) |> mutate(Model=nm)
}))
top5<-head(order(cooks.distance(model5),decreasing=TRUE),5)
model5_drop1<-glm(f5,data=d_assess[-top5[1],],family=binomial())
model5_drop5<-glm(f5,data=d_assess[-top5,],family=binomial())
model5_dedup<-glm(f5,data=d_assess[!duplicated(d_assess),],family=binomial())
model5_positive<-glm(f5,data=d_assess[d_assess$Duration_Minutes>0,],family=binomial())
sensitivity_models<-list("Full M5"=model5,"Drop largest Cook"=model5_drop1,"Drop top 5 Cook"=model5_drop5,
  "Remove exact duplicate rows"=model5_dedup,"Positive duration only"=model5_positive,"Omit exit rate"=model5_noexit,"Flexible administrative count"=model5_admin)
sensitivity_contrasts<-bind_rows(lapply(names(sensitivity_models),function(nm) {
  bind_rows(lapply(levels(d_assess$VisitorType),function(v) duration_contrast(sensitivity_models[[nm]],v))) |> mutate(Analysis=nm)
}))

# Original conditional predictions use 18 pages. Examine an approximate local
# support window, then restrict the revised figure to 5-25 min for BOTH groups.
prediction_support<-d_assess |> filter(ProductRelated>=15,ProductRelated<=21) |>
  group_by(VisitorType) |> summarise(Sessions=n(),P95_minutes=quantile(Duration_Minutes,.95),
    Maximum_minutes=max(Duration_Minutes),Sessions_60plus=sum(Duration_Minutes>=60),.groups="drop")
prediction_grid<-expand.grid(Duration_Minutes=seq(5,25,length.out=151),VisitorType=levels(d_assess$VisitorType))
prediction_grid$VisitorType<-factor(prediction_grid$VisitorType,levels=levels(d_assess$VisitorType))
prediction_grid$Log_Duration<-log1p(prediction_grid$Duration_Minutes)
prediction_grid$ProductRelated<-18
prediction_grid$Weekend<-factor(FALSE,levels=levels(d_assess$Weekend))
prediction_grid$Administrative<-median(d_assess$Administrative)
prediction_grid$Informational<-median(d_assess$Informational)
prediction_grid$ExitRates<-median(d_assess$ExitRates)
prediction_grid$Month<-factor("May",levels=levels(d_assess$Month))
prediction_grid$TrafficGroup<-factor("2",levels=levels(d_assess$TrafficGroup))
pr<-predict(model5,newdata=prediction_grid,type="link",se.fit=TRUE)
prediction_grid$Probability<-plogis(pr$fit)
prediction_grid$Lower<-plogis(pr$fit-1.96*pr$se.fit)
prediction_grid$Upper<-plogis(pr$fit+1.96*pr$se.fit)
probability_plot<-ggplot(prediction_grid,aes(Duration_Minutes,Probability,color=VisitorType,fill=VisitorType)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=Lower,ymax=Upper),alpha=.12,color=NA) + geom_line(linewidth=.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::label_percent(accuracy=1)) +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("#156082","#BD582C"),labels=visitor_labels) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("#156082","#BD582C"),labels=visitor_labels) +
  labs(x="Product browsing duration (minutes)",y="Conditional purchase probability",color=NULL,fill=NULL) +
  theme(legend.position="bottom")

calibration_data<-diagnostic_rows |> group_by(Model) |> mutate(Bin=ntile(Fitted,10)) |>
  group_by(Model,Bin) |> summarise(Predicted=mean(Fitted),Observed=mean(d_assess$Revenue[Row]),N=n(),.groups="drop")
calibration_plot<-ggplot(calibration_data,aes(Predicted,Observed,color=Model)) + geom_abline(slope=1,intercept=0,linetype=2) +
  geom_point(size=2) + geom_line() + coord_equal() + labs(x="Mean fitted probability",y="Observed conversion rate") +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("#6A6A6A","#156082"))
roc_objects<-lapply(models_assess[c("M2","M5")],function(m) pROC::roc(d_assess$Revenue,fitted(m),levels=c(0,1),direction="<",quiet=TRUE))
roc_data<-bind_rows(lapply(names(roc_objects),function(nm) tibble(Model=nm,FPR=1-roc_objects[[nm]]$specificities,TPR=roc_objects[[nm]]$sensitivities)))
roc_plot<-ggplot(roc_data,aes(FPR,TPR,color=Model)) + geom_line(linewidth=.8) +
  geom_abline(slope=1,intercept=0,linetype=2) + coord_equal() +
  labs(x="1 - specificity",y="Sensitivity") + scale_color_manual(values=c("#6A6A6A","#156082"))
# No threshold tuning or train/test exercise: inference is the project goal.
# 0.5 is a transparent illustrative equal-cost threshold for calibrated probabilities.
# It is not claimed to be optimal for an unspecified business decision.
thresholds<-c(.5,mean(d_assess$Revenue))
classification<-bind_rows(lapply(thresholds,function(t) {
  actual<-d_assess$Revenue;pred<-as.integer(fitted(model5)>=t)
  TP<-sum(pred==1 & actual==1);TN<-sum(pred==0 & actual==0)
  FP<-sum(pred==1 & actual==0);FN<-sum(pred==0 & actual==1)
  tibble(Threshold=t,TP=TP,FP=FP,FN=FN,TN=TN,Sensitivity=TP/(TP+FN),Specificity=TN/(TN+FP),
    PPV=TP/(TP+FP),Accuracy=(TP+TN)/length(actual))
}))
confusion<-with(classification[1,],matrix(c(TN,FP,FN,TP),nrow=2,byrow=TRUE,
  dimnames=list(Actual=c("No purchase","Purchase"),Predicted=c("No purchase","Purchase"))))

# Publication tables use exponential scale; SE(OR) is a delta-method SE.
nice_term<-function(z) {
  z<-gsub("splines::ns(Log_Duration, df = 3)","Duration spline basis ",z,fixed=TRUE)
  z<-gsub("VisitorTypeReturning_Visitor","Returning visitor",z,fixed=TRUE)
  z<-gsub("Duration_Minutes","Duration (min)",z,fixed=TRUE)
  z<-gsub("ProductRelated","Product pages (count)",z,fixed=TRUE)
  z<-gsub("Administrative","Administrative pages (count)",z,fixed=TRUE)
  z<-gsub("Informational","Informational pages (count)",z,fixed=TRUE)
  z<-gsub("ExitRates","Exit rate (proportion)",z,fixed=TRUE)
  z<-gsub("WeekendTRUE","Weekend vs weekday",z,fixed=TRUE)
  z<-gsub("TrafficGroupOther","Traffic: pooled sparse categories",z,fixed=TRUE)
  z<-gsub("TrafficGroup","Traffic code ",z,fixed=TRUE)
  z<-gsub("Month","Month: ",z,fixed=TRUE)
  z<-gsub(":"," x ",z,fixed=TRUE)
  z<-gsub("(Intercept)","Intercept",z,fixed=TRUE)
  z
}
coef_table<-function(m) {
  ss<-coef(summary(m));beta<-ss[,1];se<-ss[,2]
  tibble(Predictor=nice_term(rownames(ss)),`Exp(estimate)`=sprintf("%.4g",exp(beta)),
    `SE exp-scale`=sprintf("%.3g",exp(beta)*se),
    `95% CI`=sprintf("%.3g to %.3g",exp(beta-1.96*se),exp(beta+1.96*se)),`p-value`=fmt_p(ss[,4]))
}
table_fit<-fit_metrics |> transmute(Model,Parameters,Deviance=round(Deviance,1),AIC=round(AIC,1),
  `McFadden R2`=round(McFadden,3),`HL p`=fmt_p(HL_p))
table_contrast<-contrast_table |> filter(Model %in% c("M2","M4","M5")) |>
  transmute(Model,Visitor=dplyr::recode(Visitor,!!!visitor_labels),`OR: 10 to 20 min`=sprintf("%.2f",OR),
    `95% CI`=sprintf("%.2f to %.2f",Lower,Upper))
for(nm in c("fit_metrics","interaction_tests","functional_tests","vif_main","vif_interaction","vif_proposed",
  "numerical_checks","category_support","influence_summary","contrast_table","sensitivity_contrasts",
  "prediction_support","classification","calibration_data")) {
  write.csv(get(nm),file.path("outputs/diagnostics",paste0(nm,".csv")),row.names=FALSE)
}
write.csv(predictor_cor,"outputs/diagnostics/predictor_correlations.csv")
write.csv(coef_table(model5),"outputs/diagnostics/proposed_model_coefficients.csv",row.names=FALSE)
for(nm in c("partial_initial_plot","partial_log_plot","residual_plot","cook_plot","probability_plot","calibration_plot","roc_plot")) {
  ggsave(file.path("outputs/diagnostics",paste0(nm,".png")),get(nm),width=7,height=3.5,dpi=180,bg="white")
}
saveRDS(list(models=models_assess,fit_metrics=fit_metrics,contrasts=contrast_table),"outputs/diagnostics/model_assessment.rds")
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()),"outputs/diagnostics/session-info.txt")


```

# Part I. Data science memo

**To:** E-commerce product manager  
**Subject:** Visitor engagement and purchase conversion  
**Status:** Analysis draft; proposed model revision requires team review

## Executive summary

We studied 12,245 sessions to assess whether product browsing time relates to
purchase conversion differently for new and returning visitors, after accounting
for other session characteristics. New visitors converted more often than
returning visitors (24.91% versus 13.93%), despite shorter average product
browsing time. Duration and conversion are associated, but the estimated
visitor-group difference depends on how duration and other behaviors are modeled.

The original linear-duration model suggested a stronger positive association for
new visitors. Diagnostics identified functional-form and calibration concerns.
Broader adjustment and a flexible duration specification give evidence that the
relationship's shape differs by visitor type (joint interaction p
`r fmt_p(interaction_tests$p[4])`). A simpler log-duration alternative does not
clearly distinguish the two slopes (p `r fmt_p(interaction_tests$p[3])`). These
results do not establish that increasing time on site causes purchases. Use the
findings to guide investigation and experiments, while reviewing the proposed
specification before adopting a single numerical effect.

## Motivation and descriptive findings

Browsing can reflect both interest and comparison shopping. Sakar and colleagues
(2019) show that session behavior can inform purchase-intention analysis.
For a product manager, the practical question is whether the same engagement
measure has the same interpretation across visitor groups.

**Research question:** How does the relationship between product-page engagement
and purchase conversion differ between new and returning visitors, after
accounting for other browsing behaviors and session characteristics?

```{r}
#| label: memo-descriptive-table
df_clean |> group_by(VisitorType) |>
  summarise(Sessions=n(),Purchases=sum(Revenue),Conversion=scales::percent(mean(Revenue),accuracy=.01),
    `Mean time (min)`=round(mean(Duration_Minutes),2),.groups="drop") |>
  mutate(VisitorType=dplyr::recode(VisitorType,!!!visitor_labels)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names=c("Visitor type","Sessions","Purchases","Conversion","Mean time (min)"),booktabs=TRUE)
```

Overall conversion was 15.45%. These group comparisons are descriptive and do
not adjust for differing session composition. The stakeholder should interpret
time alongside navigation volume and acquisition context.

\newpage

## Statistical findings and interpretation

```{r}
#| label: fig-memo-probability
#| fig-cap: "Proposed model: conditional purchase probabilities with pointwise 95% confidence intervals. Profile: 18 product pages, weekday, May, traffic code 2, other page counts and exit rate at medians."
#| fig-width: 6.3
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-pos: H
probability_plot
```

The revised curves allow the duration-conversion association to change across
the observed range. They describe a specified session profile, rather than
average probabilities for every visitor. Displaying only 5-25 minutes avoids
zero-time extrapolation for this 18-page profile and the earlier unsupported
60-minute illustration for new visitors with roughly
18 product pages. Joint support for all characteristics is still imperfect.

```{r}
#| label: memo-contrast-table
table_contrast |> filter(Model=="M5") |> select(-Model) |>
  knitr::kable(booktabs=TRUE,caption="Proposed-model odds ratios for 10 versus 20 minutes, holding other characteristics constant.")
```

Odds ratios compare purchase odds; they are not probability ratios. Because the
model is nonlinear, this contrast does not apply to every additional ten minutes.
The overall interaction compares entire curve shapes, not only this interval.

## High-level methodology and recommended next steps

We used logistic regression for a binary purchase outcome, including an
interaction between duration and visitor type. We compared the original models
with broader adjustment for navigation, month and traffic category. Model
assessment motivated a flexible duration specification. Findings are exploratory
associations from a historical observational dataset.

Investigate whether new and returning visitors need different navigation or
product-information support. Do not set a universal time-on-site target from
these results. Test proposed changes in a randomized experiment and measure
conversion, while monitoring customer experience. Before operational use,
collect intent, product, price and campaign information, verify the specification
with the team, and assess performance on new sessions.

\newpage

# Part II. Technical appendix

## Data, study population and assumptions

The UCI dataset contains 12,330 sessions and 18 original variables (Sakar &
Kastro, 2018). Its documentation states that sessions were sampled from different
users over a year. We exclude 85 sessions labeled as the other visitor category
because the question concerns new versus returning visitors. No missing-value
imputation is needed. The analytical sample has 1,892 purchases and 10,353
non-purchases. Durations are converted from seconds to minutes. Zero durations
and long sessions are retained because they are not, by themselves, data errors.

There are 125 duplicate rows in the original data and
`r sum(duplicated(d_assess))` in the analytical sample. Without identifiers, their
status cannot be verified; they are retained with a deduplication sensitivity
analysis. Distinct sampled users support independence, but cannot rule out
shared campaign or time effects. The binary outcome is compatible with a
Bernoulli distribution. Logistic regression assumes the specified mean structure
on the log-odds scale; it does not require normal predictors or normal residuals.

## Model specification and adjustment rationale

Let $Y_i$ indicate a purchase, $D_i$ denote product browsing minutes, and $R_i$
indicate a returning visitor. The two original models are

$$\operatorname{logit}(p_i)=\beta_0+\beta_D D_i+\beta_R R_i+
\beta_P P_i+\beta_W W_i \quad (M1),$$
$$\operatorname{logit}(p_i)=\beta_0+\beta_D D_i+\beta_R R_i+
\beta_{DR}D_iR_i+\beta_P P_i+\beta_W W_i \quad (M2),$$

where $P_i$ is product page count and $W_i$ indicates weekend. M3 adds month,
traffic category, administrative and informational page counts, and exit rate.
M4 replaces $D_i$ with $\log(1+D_i)$. The proposed M5 is

$$\operatorname{logit}(p_i)=\alpha+\gamma R_i+
\sum_{k=1}^{3}\{\theta_k B_k[\log(1+D_i)]
+\delta_k R_i B_k[\log(1+D_i)]\}+\boldsymbol{\eta}^{T}\mathbf{C}_i,$$

where $B_k$ are natural-spline basis functions and $\mathbf C_i$ contains the
M3 controls. The spline uses 3 degrees of freedom, interior knots at the
one-third and two-thirds quantiles, and observed boundaries. The joint null is
$\delta_1=\delta_2=\delta_3=0$.

Controls represent navigation volume, seasonal context and acquisition source;
they are plausible adjustment variables rather than verified causal confounders.
Traffic codes with fewer than 100 sessions are pooled by frequency alone. Page
value is omitted because it is transaction-related; bounce rate is omitted
because of its overlap with exit rate. An alternate model omits exit rate because
it may reflect the same browsing process. References are new visitors, weekdays,
May and traffic code 1. All models use maximum likelihood on the same sessions.

\newpage

## Functional form, correlation and numerical checks

```{r}
#| label: fig-appendix-partial
#| fig-cap: "Initial model partial residual checks: LOESS (solid) and a linear guide (dashed). Display is trimmed; fitted models retain all observations."
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-pos: H
partial_initial_plot + labs(title=NULL)
```

The original model's nonlinear-duration check rejects the constant-slope
restriction (LR p `r fmt_p(functional_tests$p[1])`). A log transform is considered
after this assessment, not to normalize the predictor. M4 improves AIC over M3
by `r round(AIC(model3)-AIC(model4),1)`, but a nested comparison still favors
duration curvature in M5 (LR `r round(functional_tests$LR[3],2)`, 4 df,
p `r fmt_p(functional_tests$p[3])`). Raw and log models are nonnested, so no
likelihood-ratio test is used between them.

Duration and product page count correlate at
`r round(predictor_cor['Duration_Minutes','ProductRelated'],3)`.
Their M1 VIFs are `r round(vif_main$VIF[1],2)` and
`r round(vif_main$VIF[3],2)`. M2 duration and interaction term VIFs are
`r round(vif_interaction$VIF[1],1)` and `r round(vif_interaction$VIF[5],1)`;
these also reflect overlap between interaction columns and the unequal visitor
group sizes. The interaction is retained to address the research question.
Multi-column GVIFs and correlations are exported with the diagnostic results.

All five model fits converge with full-rank design matrices. Tighter-tolerance
refits, coefficient standard errors and extreme probabilities are inspected.
Both outcomes occur in each retained categorical level after pooling. There is
no obvious numerical separation warning in M5; this screen is not a formal proof
that separation is absent. The course's HW6 motivates partial residual and
Hosmer-Lemeshow checks; the GLM slides guide the distribution and link assumptions.

Remaining functional-form checks are exploratory: administrative page count has
evidence of curvature (p `r fmt_p(functional_tests$p[functional_tests$Comparison=="M5: curvature in Administrative"])`).
Its flexible sensitivity model is assessed alongside case deletion and
deduplication. Other unmodeled interactions may remain; M5 is a reviewable
proposal rather than a claim that every assumption has been verified.

\newpage

## Model comparison and interaction inference

```{r}
#| label: appendix-fit-table
knitr::kable(table_fit,booktabs=TRUE)
```

M1/M2 use the original adjustment; M3 expands adjustment; M4 changes duration
scale; M5 allows nonlinear duration effects. McFadden's pseudo-$R^2$ compares
log likelihoods with an intercept-only model and is not variance explained.
Hosmer-Lemeshow uses ten fitted-risk groups; a nonsignificant result does not
establish correctness, and its result depends on grouping and sample size.

```{r}
#| label: appendix-interaction-table
interaction_tests |> transmute(Comparison,df,LR=round(LR,2),`p-value`=fmt_p(p)) |>
  knitr::kable(booktabs=TRUE)
```

The initial interaction LR statistic is `r round(interaction_tests$LR[1],2)`
(1 df). Its per-minute odds ratios are approximately 1.0255 for new visitors
and 1.0046 for returning visitors, conditional on page count and weekend.
Those estimates should not be carried into the revised model unchanged.

After expansion and a simple log-duration specification, interaction evidence
weakens (M4 p `r fmt_p(interaction_tests$p[3])`). M5's joint test instead detects
differences in nonlinear shapes (3 df, p `r fmt_p(interaction_tests$p[4])`).
These tests evaluate different restrictions. The data support exploring visitor
differences, but do not justify a single universal extra per-minute effect for
new visitors. All specification choices and subsequent uncertainty estimates
are exploratory; nominal intervals do not account for model selection.

Finite 10-to-20-minute contrasts in the memo use the full coefficient covariance
matrix: for design-row difference $\Delta x$, the log odds ratio is
$\Delta x^T\hat\beta$ and its standard error is
$\sqrt{\Delta x^T\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)\Delta x}$.
Predicted intervals are formed on the logit scale and inverse-transformed.
Full original-M2 and proposed-M5 coefficient tables appear in the supplementary
tables, referenced here because spline coefficients are basis parameters and
must not be interpreted as individual per-minute effects.

\newpage

## Residuals, influence and calibration

```{r}
#| label: fig-appendix-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Binary outcomes generate two residual bands. Their existence is not a normality violation."
#| fig-width: 6.3
#| fig-height: 2.0
#| fig-pos: H
residual_plot
```

Cook's distance flags `r influence_summary$Flagged[1]` M2 sessions and
`r influence_summary$Flagged[2]` M5 sessions above $4/n$; this is an investigation
rule, not an exclusion rule. Maximum Cook's distances are
`r round(influence_summary$Max_Cook[1],3)` and
`r round(influence_summary$Max_Cook[2],3)`. Actual refits remove the largest
one/five M5 cases and exact duplicate rows. The original sample remains primary.
A positive-duration-only sensitivity fit also checks dependence on zero-time records.

```{r}
#| label: appendix-sensitivity-table
sensitivity_contrasts |> filter(Analysis %in% c("Full M5","Drop largest Cook","Drop top 5 Cook","Remove exact duplicate rows")) |>
  transmute(Analysis,Visitor=dplyr::recode(Visitor,!!!visitor_labels),
    `OR: 10 to 20 min`=sprintf("%.2f",OR),`95% CI`=sprintf("%.2f to %.2f",Lower,Upper)) |>
  knitr::kable(booktabs=TRUE)
```

These checks assess finite contrasts rather than comparing spline basis
coefficients across refits. Re-estimated bases can change coefficient scales.
Omitting exit rate and allowing flexible administrative page counts are
additional exported sensitivities. Statistical significance alone does not
resolve whether these variables belong in the adjustment set.

```{r}
#| label: fig-appendix-calibration
#| fig-cap: "In-sample calibration by fitted-risk deciles; the diagonal denotes agreement."
#| fig-width: 4.2
#| fig-height: 1.6
#| fig-pos: H
calibration_plot
```

## Secondary classification assessment

```{r}
#| label: fig-appendix-roc
#| fig-cap: "In-sample ROC curves; predictive assessment is secondary to inference."
#| fig-width: 3.4
#| fig-height: 1.6
#| fig-pos: H
roc_plot
```

Apparent AUC is `r round(fit_metrics$AUC[2],3)` for M2 and
`r round(fit_metrics$AUC[5],3)` for M5. These are development-sample metrics,
not estimates of future performance. A 0.50 threshold illustrates an equal-cost
classification decision for calibrated probabilities; no intervention costs were
provided to identify a business optimum. At this threshold, sensitivity is
`r scales::percent(classification$Sensitivity[1],accuracy=.1)` and specificity
is `r scales::percent(classification$Specificity[1],accuracy=.1)`.

```{r}
#| label: appendix-confusion-table
knitr::kable(confusion,booktabs=TRUE,caption="Actual outcome (rows) versus predicted outcome (columns), threshold 0.50.")
```

Lowering the threshold to the observed prevalence
(`r round(classification$Threshold[2],3)`) gives sensitivity
`r scales::percent(classification$Sensitivity[2],accuracy=.1)` and specificity
`r scales::percent(classification$Specificity[2],accuracy=.1)`.
An always-no-purchase rule is already 84.55% accurate. We therefore avoid treating
accuracy as evidence of model adequacy or spending substantial effort on tuning.

## Limitations, future work and review decisions

Purchase intent, product mix, price, campaign definitions and several session
features remain uncontrolled. Conditioning on navigation or exit rate may remove
part of the browsing process. Measurement timing is not sufficient to establish
causal direction. One historical website and the exclusion of the other visitor
category limit generalization. User IDs and exact dates are unavailable, and
very long new-visitor sessions are sparse. Calibration and diagnostics use the
same sample as estimation; model selection adds unaccounted uncertainty.

**Before submission:** confirm the broader covariate set and spline specification
with Person 2; reconcile the original slope statements with the revised curves;
review the alternate adjustment results; incorporate any new professor feedback;
and obtain all three members' review. Collect identifiers, timestamps, product,
price and intent measures, and use a randomized design for causal product decisions.

**References.** Sakar, C. O., & Kastro, Y. (2018). *Online shoppers purchasing
intention dataset*. UCI. <https://doi.org/10.24432/C5F88Q>.
Sakar et al. (2019). *Neural Computing and Applications, 31*, 6893-6908.
<https://doi.org/10.1007/s00521-018-3523-0>.
Lane, A. (2026). IDS 702 GLM, logistic-estimation and odds slides; Homework 6
(course materials). R Core Team. *Regression deletion diagnostics*.
<https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-patched/library/stats/html/influence.measures.html>.
